question.text: A medium-sized office (3,000 m2) shows electricity consumption stable at ~45,000 kWh/month for nine months, then a step change to ~62,000 kWh/month for the last three months. Gas consumption shows a normal seasonal pattern. Identify the most likely cause and one diagnostic step.
question.context: Step-change anomaly in electricity only, no gas change.

answer.text: Step change of ~17,000 kWh/month sustained for 3 months indicates a new electric load commissioned ~3 months ago — likely server room, supplementary cooling, or kitchen equipment. Gas being unaffected rules out heating control change. Diagnostic step: cross-reference the step-change date against IT or M&E project completions, then sub-meter to isolate the new load.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM22 Energy assessment and reporting methodology; ESOS Phase 4 guidance

rubric.criterion: Identifies new electrical load as primary cause
Notes gas being stable rules out heating issue
Recommends diagnostic step (sub-metering or project cross-reference)

question.text: A school's gas consumption profile shows summer-month base load of 8,000 kWh/month (July-August) when school is unoccupied. Heating season profile is normal. Identify the likely cause and remediation.
question.context: Unexpected summer gas base load in unoccupied building.

answer.text: 8,000 kWh/month summer gas in an unoccupied school indicates the boiler is firing during summer — likely a control fault: failed time-clock, missing seasonal hold-off, or the BMS optimum-start not respecting holiday calendar. Could also be DHW circulation pump running continuously. Remediation: check boiler-enable signal during summer, verify holiday calendar in BMS, isolate boilers during unoccupied periods, and provide DHW from immersion or point-of-use heaters in summer.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM39 Building energy metering; CIBSE Guide H Building Controls

rubric.criterion: Identifies boiler firing during unoccupied period as cause
References control / seasonal hold-off issue
Recommends BMS holiday calendar / boiler isolation

question.text: An office building's electricity bill suddenly shows 12,500 kWh consumed in a single billing period vs typical 8,000 kWh for the same month last year. The invoice notes a 'meter estimated reading'. Building is occupied normally. Identify whether this is a billing anomaly or operational anomaly, and recommend action.
question.context: Estimated reading + apparent step increase.

answer.text: Estimated readings are unreliable — supplier estimates based on a previous profile and can overshoot. Before treating this as an operational issue, request a customer-supplied actual meter reading and have the supplier re-bill. If the actual reading confirms ~12,500 kWh, investigate further (control fault, plant runtime); if actual is ~8,500 kWh, this was a billing anomaly. ESOS recommends actual readings monthly for all sites > 500 kW.
answer.citation: Ofgem billing rules; CIBSE TM39 sub-metering; ESOS Phase 4 guidance

rubric.criterion: Identifies estimated-reading flag as likely billing anomaly
Recommends actual meter reading before further investigation
References supplier rebill / Ofgem process

question.text: A retail unit's electricity profile shows weekday daytime peak at ~25 kW (consistent), but weekend daytime peak has risen from ~5 kW to ~18 kW over the last six months. Trading hours have not changed. Identify likely cause and remediation.
question.context: Weekend daytime base-load creep with no operational change.

answer.text: Weekend daytime 5 -> 18 kW with no trading change suggests HVAC or refrigeration is running during unoccupied weekend daytime — possibly a BMS schedule override that was never reverted, a failed time-switch, or new always-on equipment (e.g. tenant fit-out left a system on). Remediation: review BMS weekend schedule, check for override flags, walk the site on a Saturday afternoon to identify running plant, and reset schedules. ~13 kW for 16 hours/weekend = ~10,800 kWh/year wasted, ~£2,000-3,000 saving potential at 2026 retail prices.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM39; ESOS Phase 4; Carbon Trust retail benchmarks

rubric.criterion: Identifies weekend BMS schedule / always-on plant as likely cause
Recommends site walk or schedule audit
Quantifies energy / cost impact

question.text: A care home shows gas consumption 22,000 kWh in October, 35,000 kWh in November, 31,000 kWh in December — typical heating season. January spike to 58,000 kWh. February returns to 30,000 kWh. Outdoor temperature was normal across the period. Identify likely cause.
question.context: Single-month gas spike in heating season.

answer.text: Single-month doubling of gas consumption with normal weather suggests either a brief but significant fault (e.g. valve stuck open on a heating zone, hot water cylinder overheating, frost-protection relay stuck), a meter misread (check if December or February were estimated), or a brief tenant complaint period addressed by leaving heating boost on. Remediation: pull half-hourly gas data for January, identify whether the over-consumption was steady or in spikes, and check maintenance/works records for that month.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM39; CIBSE TM22

rubric.criterion: Identifies plausible cause (fault, override, meter misread)
Recommends half-hourly data drill-down
Notes weather-correction or meter check

question.text: A small office's monthly electricity bills for the past 12 months show: Jan-Aug ~6,000 kWh/month, Sep 9,500, Oct 9,200, Nov 9,400, Dec 8,800 (Christmas reduction). The increase appears in autumn-winter. No heating system on electricity (gas heating). Identify likely cause.
question.context: Seasonal autumn-winter rise in electricity not driven by heating.

answer.text: An autumn-winter electricity rise in a gas-heated building of ~3,000-3,500 kWh/month points to lighting. UK daylight hours fall from 16 to 8 between summer and winter, doubling artificial lighting use. ~3,000 kWh/month extra is consistent with ~10 hours/day of additional artificial lighting at ~10 kW total load over a 30-day month. Remediation: check daylight-linked dimming controls (often disabled), install or recommission them, and ensure occupancy sensors operate correctly. Could save 30-50% of the increment.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide A daylighting; CIBSE LG14 lighting controls

rubric.criterion: Identifies lighting as cause (daylight hours)
Rules out heating via electricity
Recommends daylight-dimming or occupancy controls

question.text: A leisure centre's gas consumption has a stable monthly trend, but the unit rate on the invoice has jumped from 4.5p/kWh to 18p/kWh in October. Consumption is normal. Identify whether this is an operational, billing, or commercial anomaly.
question.context: Unit rate quadrupled with stable consumption.

answer.text: This is a commercial anomaly: a fixed-price contract has likely expired and the supplier has placed the meter on 'out of contract' or 'deemed' rates, which are punitive (typically 3-5x normal rates). Action: contact supplier immediately, request return to in-contract rates retrospectively where possible, and procure a new gas contract via broker or direct negotiation. Out-of-contract sites should be flagged in any portfolio reviews — common cause of cost overruns. Operational and consumption are fine; do not investigate plant.
answer.citation: Ofgem business supply rules; CIBSE Energy Performance Certificates guidance

rubric.criterion: Identifies out-of-contract / deemed-rate cause
Distinguishes commercial from operational anomaly
Recommends contract renegotiation

question.text: A manufacturing facility's electricity profile shows a typical 24/5 schedule (Mon-Fri 24-hour, weekend off). Recent 12 months show weekend base load creeping from ~50 kW to ~85 kW. Plant is supposedly fully shut down at weekends. Identify likely cause.
question.context: Creeping weekend base load in supposedly shut industrial site.

answer.text: Weekend base load of 85 kW = 'parasitic' load that should not exist. Likely causes: compressed-air leaks (compressors cycling at weekends), pumps/fans left running due to faulty time-switches or BMS override, refrigeration or chilled-water systems maintaining setpoints unnecessarily, IT/server infrastructure (legitimate but worth quantifying), or transformer no-load losses. Remediation: install a sub-meter on weekend base loads, conduct an air-leak audit (ultrasonic), set up a 'weekend walk' procedure to verify shutdowns. ~35 kW reduction over 5,000 weekend hours = ~175,000 kWh/year savings.
answer.citation: Carbon Trust industrial energy guide; ESOS Phase 4 audit methodology

rubric.criterion: Identifies parasitic load drivers (compressors, pumps, etc.)
Recommends sub-metering or leak audit
Quantifies savings opportunity

question.text: A hotel with consistent occupancy shows electricity consumption normal at ~80,000 kWh/month for 11 months, then 215,000 kWh in August. No plant changes, building has chillers for air conditioning. Outdoor August temperatures were the warmest on record. Identify likely cause.
question.context: Summer cooling spike during heatwave.

answer.text: Most likely a legitimate cooling spike driven by extreme summer temperatures — chiller energy is highly sensitive to outdoor wet-bulb temperature. A 2.7x consumption increase in August during a record heatwave is large but plausible if base load is dominated by chiller-free months. Recommendation: weather-normalise consumption using cooling degree days to confirm proportionality; if even weather-corrected consumption is anomalous, investigate chiller efficiency, possible refrigerant loss, or controls strategy. Look at refrigerant leak detection if 2x exceeds CDD ratio.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM41 Degree days; CIBSE TM44 Inspection of air conditioning systems

rubric.criterion: Identifies cooling-driven legitimate spike during heatwave
Recommends weather-normalisation via CDD
Notes refrigerant / efficiency check if disproportionate

source.primary: CIBSE TM41 Degree days; CIBSE TM44

question.text: A multi-tenant office's communal electricity (lifts, common-area lighting, landlord plant) was historically ~12,000 kWh/month. The bill now shows 22,000 kWh/month sustained for 4 months. Tenants pay separately. Identify likely causes (top three) and diagnostic approach.
question.context: Sustained doubling of landlord/communal electricity.

answer.text: Top three likely causes: (1) tenant electricity being incorrectly billed to landlord — check meter mapping after recent tenant change; (2) ventilation/AHU running extended hours (BMS schedule change or override); (3) lift modernisation or new chiller commissioned and now serving common areas. Diagnostic: pull half-hourly profile to identify time-of-day signature (continuous = always-on plant, AM/PM peaks = ventilation/lifts, evening base = security/emergency lighting). Compare to known plant inventory.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM39; landlord-tenant metering guidance

rubric.criterion: Identifies tenant-billing-misallocation as a possibility
Identifies plant operation change
Recommends half-hourly profile analysis

question.text: A 5,000 m2 city centre office (typical electricity ~110 kWh/m2/yr) shows half-hourly data with overnight base load creeping from 18 kW (Jan) to 34 kW (Jun) with no occupancy change. Daytime peak remains at 140 kW. The IT manager mentions a new in-house data analytics platform was deployed in February. Identify the most likely cause and recommend a diagnostic step.
question.context: Gradual overnight base-load creep coinciding with IT project.

answer.text: Primary cause: server room / comms room load growth — the new analytics platform has added always-on compute (servers + supplementary CRAC cooling), driving overnight base load up by ~16 kW (~140,000 kWh/yr, ~£35k at 25p/kWh). Evidence: the creep starts at the platform deployment, is sustained overnight (when only 24/7 loads run), and daytime peak is unchanged because daytime load is dominated by occupancy. Diagnostic: install a temporary sub-meter on the comms room distribution board (or read existing sub-meter trends), measure server room PUE, and review IT virtualisation / decommissioning opportunities. If PUE > 2.0, investigate CRAC setpoints and hot/cold aisle containment.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM22; CIBSE Guide F; BCO Guide to Specification; EU Code of Conduct for Data Centres

rubric.criterion: Identifies IT/server room growth as primary cause
Links overnight base-load pattern to 24/7 IT load and rules out occupancy
Recommends sub-metering or PUE diagnostic

source.primary: CIBSE TM22; EU Code of Conduct for Data Centres

question.text: A 2,200 m2 suburban office shows weekend (Sat+Sun) electricity consumption rising from ~600 kWh/weekend in January to ~1,650 kWh/weekend by July. Weekday consumption is stable at ~2,800 kWh/day. The building is unoccupied at weekends and the BMS schedule is set to 07:00-18:00 Mon-Fri. Outside air temperatures rose seasonally. Identify likely cause and remediation.
question.context: Weekend creep correlating with summer temperatures.

answer.text: Primary cause: AHU/chiller plant running at weekends due to optimum-start, free-cooling, or frost-protection routines being triggered, or a manual BMS override left in place. Evidence: weekend consumption tracks outdoor temperature (summer rise), suggesting cooling plant is the driver rather than IT or lighting (which would be flat year-round). The ~1,050 kWh/weekend uplift (~55,000 kWh/yr, ~£14k at 25p/kWh) is consistent with a 30-40 kW chiller running intermittently. Diagnostic: review BMS schedule and override log, check optimum-start parameters, confirm setback setpoints (e.g. cooling setback to 28°C), and conduct a Saturday afternoon site walk to identify running plant. Implement weekend lockout unless tenant request raised.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM39 Building energy metering; CIBSE Guide H BMS controls; Carbon Trust CTV032 Office Sector Guide

rubric.criterion: Identifies BMS schedule override / unintended weekend HVAC operation
Links temperature correlation to cooling plant (rules out IT/lighting)
Recommends BMS audit, site walk, or schedule reset

question.text: A 4,500 m2 office had electricity at ~42,000 kWh/month stable, then dropped to ~36,000 kWh/month after a lighting LED retrofit in March. In September it stepped back up to ~48,000 kWh/month with no obvious occupancy or weather change. The sub-meter for the landlord supply shows the increase, not tenant supplies. HVAC heating runs on gas. Identify likely cause and one diagnostic step.
question.context: Step-change increase on landlord sub-meter post-retrofit.

answer.text: Primary cause: a landlord-side mechanical plant change or controls drift — most likely a chiller, AHU fan, or pump running outside its intended schedule, or a heating circulation pump that has had its summer lockout removed and is now running 24/7 alongside cooling. Evidence: the 12,000 kWh/month uplift is on the landlord meter (rules out tenant equipment), gas is unaffected (rules out heating load), and timing (September) suggests an autumn changeover commissioning issue. Diagnostic: pull half-hourly profile and check whether the uplift is base-load (pump/fan always on) or daytime-only (controls issue); cross-reference BMS event log for September plant changes; sub-meter the chiller and main AHUs to isolate. Likely candidates: simultaneous heating + cooling, or a VSD reverted to fixed-speed.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM22; CIBSE TM39; CIBSE Guide H; Carbon Trust CTG005 Heating, ventilation and air conditioning

rubric.criterion: Identifies landlord HVAC plant / controls issue as primary cause
Uses landlord-sub-meter and stable gas to rule out tenant/heating causes
Recommends half-hourly profile analysis or BMS event log review

question.text: A 6,000 m2 multi-tenant office has total electricity of ~75,000 kWh/month. Sub-meters show: landlord HVAC 28,000 kWh, lighting 12,000 kWh, lifts 3,000 kWh, tenant A 14,000 kWh, tenant B 11,000 kWh — totalling 68,000 kWh. The 7,000 kWh/month gap (~9%) has grown from ~1,500 kWh/month a year ago. Identify likely cause and recommend action.
question.context: Growing unmetered residual on sub-metering reconciliation.

answer.text: Primary cause: an unmetered or wrongly-attributed load has grown over the past year — typical candidates are a comms/server room fed from the main board upstream of sub-meters, landlord small-power circuits (cleaners' sockets, signage, EV chargers), or a sub-meter that has failed/stalled and is under-reading. Evidence: the residual has grown 4.7x while total consumption is broadly stable, indicating reallocation rather than new total load; ~7,000 kWh/month (~84,000 kWh/yr) is consistent with a small server room or a ~10 kW always-on load. Diagnostic: (1) verify each sub-meter against a clamp-on portable meter for a week to check for stalled CTs or wrong multiplier; (2) trace the main LV board single-line diagram to find circuits not captured by existing sub-meters (per CIBSE TM39 metering hierarchy); (3) add sub-meters to close the gap to <5% as required for ESOS / SECR reporting confidence.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM39 Building energy metering; ESOS Phase 4 guidance; SECR reporting guidance

rubric.criterion: Identifies unmetered load or failed sub-meter as primary cause
Notes residual growth pattern points to reallocation/meter failure not new total load
Recommends portable meter check, single-line diagram review, or added sub-metering

question.text: A high-street fashion retailer (800 m2) historically consumed ~12,000 kWh/month with trading hours 09:00-18:00. From November the half-hourly profile shows consumption now extending to 22:00 weekdays and Sunday trading added, with monthly consumption at ~17,500 kWh. Lighting and HVAC remain on during all trading hours. Identify the cause and recommend an action.
question.context: Extended trading hours driving proportional consumption rise.

answer.text: Primary cause: Legitimate extended trading hours (4 extra weekday hours + Sunday opening) — ~45% extra trading hours correlates with ~46% consumption rise (12,000 -> 17,500 kWh/month), so consumption per trading hour is unchanged. Evidence: half-hourly profile shape is identical, just extended; no base-load creep visible overnight. Diagnostic/action: confirm via kWh-per-trading-hour KPI; then target reductions through occupancy-linked lighting controls, HVAC setback during the last hour of trading (pre-close), and reviewing whether full sales-floor lighting is required after 20:00. Benchmark against CIBSE Guide F retail ~320 kWh/m2/yr.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide F Energy efficiency in buildings; CIBSE TM22; Carbon Trust CTV013 retail

rubric.criterion: Identifies extended trading hours as primary cause
Supports with per-trading-hour ratio / profile shape analysis
Recommends occupancy controls or setback strategy

source.primary: CIBSE Guide F; Carbon Trust CTV013

question.text: A convenience store (250 m2) with chilled and frozen display cases shows overnight base load rising from ~8 kW (six months ago) to ~13 kW now, while daytime peak (18 kW) is unchanged. Outdoor temperatures have been mild. No new equipment has been installed. Monthly consumption up from 9,500 to 12,800 kWh. Identify likely cause and a diagnostic step.
question.context: Overnight base-load creep with stable daytime peak — refrigeration suspected.

answer.text: Primary cause: Refrigeration anomaly — most likely degraded performance across one or more cases (door-seal failure, evaporator coil icing, condenser fouling, low refrigerant charge, or stuck defrost heaters). The ~5 kW overnight rise (40 kWh/night, ~14,600 kWh/yr) shows up most clearly at night because refrigeration dominates base load when lighting/HVAC are off. Evidence: mild weather rules out ambient-driven cooling; unchanged daytime peak rules out new daytime equipment. Diagnostic: clamp-meter each refrigeration circuit overnight, inspect door gaskets and night-blinds, check condenser cleanliness, and verify defrost cycle counts via controller logs. Quick wins: night-blinds typically cut case energy 8-15%.
answer.citation: Carbon Trust CTV044 refrigeration; CIBSE TM39; F-Gas Regulation EU 517/2014

rubric.criterion: Identifies refrigeration degradation as primary cause
Rules out weather / new daytime load via profile evidence
Recommends circuit-level metering or physical inspection

question.text: A restaurant (180 m2, evening service only 17:00-23:00) shows gas consumption stable but electricity has risen from ~6,500 to ~9,200 kWh/month. Half-hourly data shows a consistent 4-5 kW load present 24/7 including all night and on Mondays when the restaurant is closed. Identify the cause and remediation.
question.context: Continuous 24/7 load on a part-time-occupied site.

answer.text: Primary cause: Kitchen extraction canopy and associated make-up air fans left running continuously — a 4-5 kW always-on load matches typical extract/MUA fan power for a small commercial kitchen, and presence on closed Mondays confirms it is not occupancy-linked. Staff likely leave the canopy switch on as 'standard procedure' or the interlock with cooking appliances has been bypassed. Evidence: gas stable (cooking unchanged), load present when kitchen is unoccupied. ~5 kW x 18 unoccupied hours x 30 days = ~2,700 kWh/month — matches the anomaly almost exactly. Remediation: install gas-interlock or VAV canopy controls (demand-controlled kitchen ventilation, DCKV) to modulate fan speed with cooking activity; retrain staff on shutdown procedure; consider a time-switch with manual override.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM50 Energy efficiency in commercial kitchens; DW/172 specification for kitchen ventilation; Carbon Trust CTG034

rubric.criterion: Identifies kitchen extract fans left running as primary cause
Uses closed-day / overnight evidence and matches kWh arithmetic
Recommends DCKV / gas interlock / staff procedure fix

question.text: A 120-bedroom city hotel (6,500 m2) with through-the-wall PTAC units in guest rooms shows July electricity consumption at 165,000 kWh, up from a typical summer ~110,000 kWh, despite stable ~78% occupancy. The week of 15-22 July saw daytime temperatures 32-35 C. Weather-normalised consumption using CDD still shows ~20% above expected. Identify the cause and a diagnostic step.
question.context: Heatwave cooling spike exceeding weather-normalised expectation.

answer.text: Primary cause: Combination of legitimate heatwave cooling load AND degraded PTAC performance / guest behaviour — base heatwave effect is expected but the 20% residual after CDD normalisation indicates inefficiency. Likely contributors: guests leaving PTACs running at low setpoints (18 C) with windows open or while out of room (no occupancy interlock), dirty filters/condenser coils reducing EER, and some units running heat-mode incorrectly. Evidence: CDD method already accounts for ambient; residual implies efficiency or control failure. Diagnostic: sample-audit 10-15 rooms during peak afternoon for setpoint, window position, filter condition, and condenser coil cleanliness; review any BMS/PMS integration for unoccupied-room setback; check refrigerant charge on a sample of units (CIBSE TM44 inspection scope). Remediation: occupancy-linked setpoint reset via key-card or door contact (typical 15-25% saving), filter cleaning cycle, and guest information cards.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM41 Degree days; CIBSE TM44; CIBSE Guide F; Carbon Trust CTV013 hospitality

rubric.criterion: Identifies combined heatwave + PTAC efficiency/control cause
Uses weather-normalised residual as evidence ruling out pure ambient effect
Recommends room audit / key-card setback / TM44 inspection

source.primary: CIBSE TM41; CIBSE TM44; Carbon Trust CTV013

question.text: A UK primary school (2,400 m2) shows electricity consumption averaging 8,500 kWh/month during term time (Sep-Jul) but the August bill shows 6,200 kWh despite the school being closed for the entire month. Gas consumption is near zero as expected. Historically August was ~2,000 kWh. Identify the most likely cause and recommend a diagnostic step.
question.context: Elevated summer holiday base load with building unoccupied.

answer.text: Primary cause: BMS/HVAC and ancillary plant continuing to run on term-time schedules during the summer holiday — likely AHUs, IT server cabinets without dedicated cooling shutdown, and corridor lighting on always-on circuits. Evidence: 6,200 kWh over 31 unoccupied days = ~8.3 kW continuous base load, ~3x the expected holiday minimum of ~2.7 kW for security/fridges/comms. Gas being zero confirms heating is off, so the load is non-heating electrical. Diagnostic: pull half-hourly data for August, identify the overnight floor (kW), then walk the site to identify running plant; review BMS holiday calendar and ensure summer setback schedules are enabled. Benchmark: CIBSE Guide F primary schools target ~32 kWh/m2/yr electricity; this site is tracking ~43 kWh/m2/yr.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM22; CIBSE Guide F Energy efficiency in buildings; Carbon Trust schools benchmark CTV019

rubric.criterion: Identifies BMS holiday schedule / always-on plant as primary cause
Uses evidence (kW base load, gas=0 ruling out heating) to support
Recommends half-hourly data review, BMS calendar audit, or site walk

source.primary: CIBSE TM22; Carbon Trust schools guide

question.text: A university lecture hall block (4,500 m2) shows electricity consumption rising from 38,000 kWh/month (Oct-Dec) to 55,000 kWh/month (Jan-Mar) despite winter term having identical timetabling. Gas use for heating is normal. Occupant complaints log shows multiple reports of 'feeling cold' in lecture theatres. Identify likely cause and recommend remediation.
question.context: Winter electricity rise with simultaneous gas heating and occupant cold complaints.

answer.text: Primary cause: cooling and heating running simultaneously — chillers or DX units overcooling the lecture theatres while the heating system reheats the supply air (classic 'fighting' control). Evidence: 17,000 kWh/month rise in winter electricity is inconsistent with a cooling-driven load unless mechanical cooling is active; cold complaints from occupants are diagnostic — overcooled spaces in winter point to failed mixed-air dampers, stuck cooling valves, or incorrect setpoints (e.g. cooling setpoint left at 19°C). Diagnostic/remediation: trend the AHU supply air temperature, cooling coil valve position, and zone temperatures via the BMS; check for stuck open chilled water valves and verify summer/winter changeover logic. Re-commission setpoints to 21-23°C heating / 24°C cooling deadband per CIBSE Guide A.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide A Environmental design; CIBSE TM39; CIBSE TM44 Inspection of air conditioning systems

rubric.criterion: Identifies simultaneous heating/cooling or overcooling as primary cause
Links occupant cold complaints and gas+electricity pattern as evidence
Recommends BMS trend review, valve check, or setpoint re-commissioning

question.text: An acute hospital (35,000 m2) with two 800 kW water-cooled chillers shows electricity consumption rising from a baseline of 480,000 kWh/month (summer 2024) to 615,000 kWh/month (summer 2025), an increase of ~28%. Outdoor temperatures and patient occupancy are within 5% of prior year. Cooling degree days are 8% higher year-on-year. Identify the likely cause and recommend a diagnostic step.
question.context: Disproportionate summer cooling load increase vs weather and occupancy.

answer.text: Primary cause: chiller efficiency degradation — likely fouled condenser tubes, refrigerant undercharge/leak, or one chiller running at low part-load while a faulty staging control prevents proper sequencing. Evidence: weather-normalising via CDD, expected rise is ~8%, but observed is 28%, so ~20 percentage points (~95,000 kWh/month) is unexplained. Occupancy stable rules out new clinical load. Diagnostic: measure chiller kW/kWr (COP) and compare against manufacturer curves at current load and condenser water temps; log refrigerant pressures and superheat; inspect condenser approach temperature (>2-3°C above design indicates fouling); review BMS chiller sequencing. Per CIBSE TM44, statutory AC inspection should flag this. Confirm refrigerant log — F-gas leak check overdue?
answer.citation: CIBSE TM41 Degree days; CIBSE TM44 Inspection of air conditioning systems; HTM 07-02 EnCO2de; F-Gas Regulation (EU) 517/2014

rubric.criterion: Identifies chiller efficiency loss (fouling, refrigerant, staging) as primary cause
Weather-normalises via CDD to rule out legitimate weather-driven rise
Recommends chiller COP measurement, refrigerant/condenser check, or TM44 inspection

question.text: A 60-bed residential care home (2,800 m2) has gas consumption that has risen from 14,000 kWh/month (2024 average) to 22,000 kWh/month (2025 same months) with no change in resident numbers, no extension built, and similar external temperatures. The home has a 1,500 litre gas-fired hot water storage cylinder serving showers, laundry, and kitchen. Heating circuit consumption is normal. Identify the most likely cause and recommend remediation.
question.context: Gas consumption rise concentrated in DHW with stable heating and occupancy.

answer.text: Primary cause: hot water cylinder losses — most likely failed/missing cylinder insulation jacket, a failed DHW secondary return pump control causing 24/7 circulation losses, scaled immersion/coil heat exchanger reducing efficiency, or a faulty thermostatic mixing valve dumping hot to drain. Evidence: 8,000 kWh/month rise (~57%) with stable heating load and occupancy points to the DHW subsystem; heating circuit normal rules out boiler/distribution. At 60 residents, typical DHW demand for a care home including laundry and catering is ~90 l/person/day at 60°C, i.e. ~9,000-12,000 kWh/month of gas — the extra 8,000 kWh implies losses doubled. Diagnostic/remediation: inspect cylinder insulation and secondary return pipework lagging (HTM 04-01); check secondary return pump runs on time-clock not continuous; descale calorifier coil; verify cylinder thermostat at 60-65°C (Legionella control limits lower bound); check for leaks/passing valves. Sub-meter the DHW gas circuit if possible.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide G Public health and plumbing; HTM 04-01 Safe water in healthcare premises; CIBSE TM39

rubric.criterion: Identifies hot water cylinder/DHW losses (insulation, secondary return, scaling) as cause
Uses heating-normal + occupancy-stable evidence to isolate DHW subsystem
Recommends inspection of insulation, secondary return control, descaling, or sub-metering

question.text: A UK metal fabrication plant (8,000 m2, single shift Mon-Fri 07:00-17:00) with a 75 kW screw compressor shows weekend/overnight electricity baseline rising from ~12 kW to ~38 kW over 8 months. Daytime peak demand unchanged at ~280 kW. Annual consumption now ~1,650 MWh vs ~1,400 MWh prior year. Identify the most likely cause and recommend a diagnostic step.
question.context: Out-of-hours baseline creep in a compressed-air-dependent facility.

answer.text: Primary cause: Compressed-air system leaks causing the compressor to cycle/load during unoccupied periods to maintain header pressure. A 26 kW out-of-hours rise corresponds closely to a ~35% loaded duty on a 75 kW compressor — typical of significant leakage (>30% of generated air). Evidence: baseline-only rise with daytime peak unchanged rules out new production loads; progressive growth over 8 months is consistent with cumulative leak development at fittings, FRLs, and quick-connects. Diagnostic: conduct a no-load/pump-up test (isolate downstream, time pressure decay) to quantify leak rate, then use ultrasonic leak detection during a shutdown to tag and repair leaks. ~26 kW x 5,000 unoccupied hours = ~130 MWh/yr (~£32k at 25p/kWh).
answer.citation: Carbon Trust CTV050 Compressed air; CIBSE TM39 Building energy metering; ISO 11011

rubric.criterion: Identifies compressed-air leaks as primary cause
Supports with baseline-only pattern and rules out new daytime load
Recommends ultrasonic leak survey or pump-up test

question.text: A refrigerated warehouse (12,000 m2, -22°C cold store) in the Midlands shows electricity consumption averaging ~310 MWh/month winter and ~410 MWh/month summer in 2024. In 2025, winter months (Jan-Mar) jumped to ~395 MWh/month despite outdoor temperatures being colder than the prior year. Throughput tonnage unchanged. Identify likely cause and recommend a diagnostic.
question.context: Cold-store winter consumption rise against colder weather — inverse correlation.

answer.text: Primary cause: Refrigeration system degradation — most likely evaporator coil icing/defrost control malfunction, condenser fouling, or refrigerant charge issue (overcharge or non-condensables). Evidence: consumption should fall in winter as condensing temperature drops (lower lift); an ~85 MWh/month rise against the expected seasonal decrease (~100 MWh) implies ~185 MWh/month of degraded performance — system COP has dropped materially. Throughput stability rules out increased product load; outdoor temp rules out ambient cause. Diagnostic: trend suction/discharge pressures and superheat, inspect evaporators for ice build-up and defrost cycle behaviour, check condenser cleanliness and fan operation, and verify door seals/strip curtains. Compare measured COP to design (~2.2-2.5 for -22°C). Consider F-Gas leak check if charge is suspect.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide F; Carbon Trust CTG046 Refrigeration; F-Gas Regulation (EU) 517/2014 retained

rubric.criterion: Identifies refrigeration plant degradation (evaporator/condenser/charge) as cause
Uses inverse seasonal correlation as evidence and rules out load/weather
Recommends pressure/superheat trending or COP check

source.primary: Carbon Trust CTG046; CIBSE Guide F

question.text: A precision machining workshop (2,500 m2) with 14 CNC machine tools shows total electricity at ~85,000 kWh/month, stable. Production data shows actual cutting/spindle time averages only 38% of machine 'on' hours; the remaining 62% is idle with spindles powered, hydraulics running, and chip conveyors cycling. Specific energy is 0.9 kWh per part vs an industry benchmark of ~0.55 kWh/part. Identify the primary cause and recommend remediation.
question.context: High parasitic / idle-state losses on machine tools.

answer.text: Primary cause: Parasitic loads on CNC machine tools during non-cutting periods — spindle drives energised, hydraulic power packs running continuously, coolant pumps, chip conveyors, and machine controllers/lighting all drawing power between cycles. Typical CNC machines draw 30-50% of peak demand at idle; with 62% idle time, idle energy can exceed cutting energy. Evidence: specific energy 64% above benchmark with low spindle utilisation directly points to non-productive consumption rather than cutting inefficiency. Diagnostic/remediation: install plug-level or circuit sub-metering on 2-3 representative machines to quantify idle vs cutting kW, implement auto power-down/sleep modes (ISO 14955-1) after configurable idle timeouts, shut hydraulics/coolant between batches, and train operators to power off at shift end. Expected savings 15-25% of machine-tool electricity.
answer.citation: ISO 14955-1 Machine tools environmental evaluation; Carbon Trust CTG067 Manufacturing; CIBSE TM39

rubric.criterion: Identifies machine-tool parasitic/idle loads as primary cause
Links low spindle utilisation and high specific energy as evidence
Recommends sub-metering and/or ISO 14955 auto-shutdown controls

question.text: A plastics injection moulding facility (5,500 m2) recorded stable electricity at ~165 MWh/month for 18 months. In April, consumption jumped to ~205 MWh/month and has held there for 3 months. Production output (tonnes of product) is unchanged. The engineering team commissioned two new all-electric moulding machines in late March, replacing two hydraulic machines of nominally similar tonnage. Identify whether this is anomalous and recommend an action.
question.context: Step-change after process-equipment replacement that was expected to save energy.

answer.text: Primary cause: The replacement is performing opposite to expectation — all-electric moulders typically use 30-60% less energy than hydraulic equivalents, so a 40 MWh/month (~24%) rise after commissioning indicates either (a) the new machines are running at incorrect setpoints (excessive barrel heat, oversized clamp force, wrong cycle parameters), (b) the old hydraulic machines were not decommissioned and are still drawing standby/parasitic power, or (c) ancillaries (chillers, dryers, granulators) were upsized or left running continuously to support the new line. Evidence: unchanged output rules out volume; the step-change date aligns with commissioning. Diagnostic: install dedicated sub-meters on the two new machines and their ancillaries, compare measured kWh/kg against manufacturer's specific energy curve, verify old machines are fully isolated, and review chiller/dryer setpoints and run schedules. Engage OEM for commissioning review if specific energy exceeds datasheet by >15%.
answer.citation: Carbon Trust CTG067 Manufacturing; CIBSE TM39; British Plastics Federation Energy Efficiency Guide

rubric.criterion: Identifies commissioning/setpoint issue or un-isolated legacy equipment as cause
Notes expected direction of change was opposite and rules out output change
Recommends sub-metering of new machines and specific-energy comparison to datasheet

source.primary: Carbon Trust CTG067; BPF Energy Efficiency Guide

question.text: A 4,500 m2 office in Manchester receives quarterly electricity bills. Q1 and Q2 consumption was 95,000 and 92,000 kWh respectively (actual reads). Q3 jumped to 178,000 kWh, but Q4 dropped to 41,000 kWh. Annual total (~406,000 kWh = 90 kWh/m2/yr) is in line with CIBSE TGD Guide F good-practice benchmark. No operational changes. Identify the cause and recommend an action.
question.context: Two consecutive quarters with opposite-direction anomalies, annual total normal.

answer.text: Primary cause: estimated reading at end of Q2 followed by an actual read at end of Q3, then another estimate or catch-up at Q4. The Q3 'spike' is the supplier reconciling underestimated Q2 usage, and Q4 is artificially low because true consumption was already billed in Q3. Evidence: annual total ~90 kWh/m2/yr matches CIBSE Guide F benchmark, and the Q3+Q4 average (~110,000 kWh) aligns with Q1/Q2 — the swing nets to zero. Diagnostic: check the 'E' vs 'A' flags on each invoice line, submit monthly customer reads via the supplier portal, and request a rebilling on actuals. Avoids false alarm investigation of plant.
answer.citation: Ofgem Standards of Conduct; CIBSE TM39 Building energy metering; CIBSE Guide F

rubric.criterion: Identifies estimated reading / reconciliation as primary cause
Uses annual total or opposite-direction swing as supporting evidence
Recommends checking E/A flags and submitting customer reads

question.text: A multi-let industrial estate has a landlord-supply meter feeding eight tenant sub-meters. The landlord bill shows 480,000 kWh for the year, but the sum of tenant sub-meter recharges is only 310,000 kWh. The unmetered common areas (external lighting, small pump room) are estimated at ~25,000 kWh/yr. One tenant, a precision engineering workshop, was recharged 18,000 kWh — similar to a neighbouring small office tenant. Identify the cause and recommend a remediation.
question.context: Large unexplained gap between landlord meter and sum of tenant sub-meters.

answer.text: Primary cause: tenant misallocation — the engineering workshop is almost certainly under-recharged because either (a) its sub-meter has been swapped or wired to the wrong tenant's CT, or (b) the multiplier/CT ratio is wrong. A workshop with CNC plant typically uses 80–200 kWh/m2/yr, not the office-like 18,000 kWh recorded. Evidence: 145,000 kWh unaccounted for after common-area allowance, and the workshop's recharge is implausibly low for its load profile. Diagnostic: walk the meter cupboard, verify each sub-meter's serial number against the recharge schedule, confirm CT ratios on the workshop meter, and consider a temporary clamp-meter log on the workshop incomer to reconcile. Issue corrected recharges once mapping is verified.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM39 Building energy metering; RICS Service Charge Code (Commercial)

rubric.criterion: Identifies tenant misallocation / sub-meter mapping error as cause
Uses load-profile mismatch or unaccounted kWh as supporting evidence
Recommends meter walk / CT ratio check / clamp-meter verification

question.text: A 1,200 m2 supermarket convenience store had its MPAN upgraded from Profile Class 04 (non-half-hourly) to half-hourly settlement in March after exceeding 100 kW maximum demand. Bills from April onward show consumption of ~38,000 kWh/month (consistent with prior year), but the total invoice cost has risen ~28% versus the same months last year despite stable unit rates. Identify the cause and recommend an action.
question.context: Cost increase post-HH conversion with consumption unchanged.

answer.text: Primary cause: post-HH-conversion charges — DUoS (red/amber/green time bands), capacity (kVA) charges, and HH data-collection/data-aggregation (DC/DA) standing charges now apply line-by-line, which were previously bundled into a simpler PC04 tariff. The kVA capacity charge in particular is often set too high at conversion (suppliers default to historical peak), inflating fixed costs. Evidence: kWh stable, unit rates stable, but invoice line items have expanded — the 28% uplift is in non-commodity components. Diagnostic: request the supplier provide an itemised HH bill, review the agreed available capacity (kVA) against actual peak demand from the HH data, and apply to the DNO for a capacity reduction if utilisation is below ~80%. Also consider shifting loads out of red-band hours (typically 16:00–19:00 weekdays in winter).
answer.citation: Ofgem DCP161 / DCP228; Elexon BSC P272; CIBSE TM39

rubric.criterion: Identifies HH-conversion non-commodity charges (DUoS / kVA capacity) as cause
Notes stable kWh and unit rates to rule out consumption or commodity price drivers
Recommends capacity review / DNO application or red-band load shifting

source.primary: Elexon BSC P272; Ofgem DUoS guidance; CIBSE TM39

question.text: A primary school (2,800 m2) had a faulty electricity meter replaced by the MOP in early September. The August bill (old meter) showed 9,200 kWh. The September bill (new meter) shows 41,500 kWh — implausible for a school in mild weather with normal occupancy. October reverts to ~10,800 kWh. Old meter final read was 184,650 kWh; new meter opening read was recorded as 00000. Identify the cause and recommend a remediation.
question.context: Single-month spike following a meter exchange.

answer.text: Primary cause: meter swap error — the supplier has billed the full new-meter register reading (~32,000 kWh of accumulated usage on the new meter, plus possibly a missed final read from the old) as September consumption, or the old meter's final read was not communicated to the supplier and they have estimated forward then 'caught up' on the new meter. Evidence: September spike (~4x normal) is isolated, October returns to ~10,800 kWh (consistent with school term reopening), and the meter exchange date coincides exactly with the anomaly. Diagnostic: obtain the MOP's meter exchange certificate showing both the old final and new opening reads, submit these to the supplier via a D0010 flow correction, and request a rebilling. Confirm new meter's MSN on subsequent bills matches the exchange certificate.
answer.citation: Elexon BSC Section L; Ofgem metering code of practice; CIBSE TM39

rubric.criterion: Identifies meter swap / register-read handover error as cause
Uses isolated single-month spike and October reversion as supporting evidence
Recommends obtaining MOP exchange certificate and supplier rebilling

source.primary: Elexon BSC Section L; CIBSE TM39
